newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore shrugs off U.S. criticism.
newsitem.headline: Singapore shrugs off U.S. criticism.

text.p: Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong has shrugged off U.S. criticism of his party's election campaign tactics and told Washington not to interfere, media reports said on Thursday.

The United States criticised Goh and candidates of his ruling People's Action Party (PAP) on Tuesday over their use of a housing upgrade programme to woo voters ahead of Singapore's January 2 general election.

The PAP, which has won every election since 1959, was returned to power before a vote was cast in next month's poll when opposition parties declared they would contest only 36 of parliament's 83 seats.
Goh told reporters at the end of a campaign walkabout on Wednesday night that he was doing only what U.S. parties did and that PAP election tactics were no business of the United States.
"First, I think foreign countries shouldn't interfere in the domestic politics of another country," The New Paper quoted Goh as saying.
"U.S. is a big country. U.S. likes to make statements all over the world, so may be it is expected of the U.S.," he said.
"But they have not understood. They've offered their own health care plans to the population, they have offered other programmes. Completely all right," Goh was quoted as saying.
"Likewise, what I am doing is to offer all these programmes to the people."
At issue was Goh's campaign statement that constituencies which elected the opposition would lose out on government housing renovations and development programmes.

"We understand that ruling party candidates, including the prime minister, have warned that constituencies that elect opposition candidates will receive low priority in extensive government plans to upgrade public housing facilities," the U.S. State Department said.

"We believe that voters everywhere should be able to vote without fear of repercussions from government as a result of their responsibilities as citizens," department press officer Sharon Bowman said in reply to a question.

Goh said on Sunday he would respect the voters' choice if they elected someone from the opposition, but added: "Then you'll be left behind; then in 20, 30 years' time, the whole of Singapore will be bustling away and your estate, through your own choice, will be left behind. They become slums. That's my message."
Information Minister George Yeo was blunter in criticising the U.S. reaction.

"I am quite surprised that the Americans should raise an issue about how we run democratic politics in Singapore when their pork-barrel politics is something of a long tradition," he told state television.
Upgrading is not the only programme the PAP has tied to victory for its candidates. Goh outlined at a Monday news conference a lengthy list of community development schemes.

"The point couldn't be simpler: the government will implement these programmes in wards where their candidates are returned; they won't be implemented where PAP candidates are voted out," a commentary in the Business Times newspaper said.
The opposition won just four seats in the last parliament, but that was its best showing since Singapore's independence in 1965.
